result:
There is a peculiar hour—around 4:47 in the morning—when the city forgets it is a city. I found myself walking through it last Tuesday, not by design but because sleep had abandoned me with the gentle cruelty of a cat leaving a dead bird on the doorstep. The streets were not empty, exactly; they were unclaimed. A single delivery truck hummed past, its driver visible only as a silhouette, and the traffic lights cycled through red and green for no one. I stood at an intersection and listened. What I heard was not silence, but the absence of argument. No horns, no footsteps in conversation, no music leaking from windows. Just the low, patient thrum of electricity in the streetlamps, and somewhere far away, the ocean of a freeway that never truly sleeps.

We build our lives in the interstices of noise. We become experts at filtering: the barista’s grinder, the notification chime, the background roar we mistake for air. But in that pre-dawn suspension, the machinery of the world reveals itself without its costume. You see the scaffolding. The garbage truck, monstrous and intimate, lifts bins with hydraulic tenderness. A baker unlocks a door, and the smell of yeast enters the street like a secret being confessed.

I think we need these moments of misalignment—when our internal clock refuses to sync with the collective rhythm. They are small rebellions. To be awake while the world dreams, or dreams while it wakes, is to remember that human time is not the only time. There is geological time, machine time, the slow metabolism of concrete and steel.

By five-thirty, the spell broke. A bus exhaled at the stop. A runner passed, earbuds in, already performing the day. I turned home, carrying the strange privilege of having witnessed the city undressed—not lonely, just alone with itself, waiting for us to arrive and make it mean something again.
